entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Seleucid Empire (312–63 BCE) was a Hellenistic state founded by Seleucus I Nicator, one of Alexander the Great's generals, after the Wars of the Diadochi that fragmented Alexander's empire. At its height the Seleucid Empire stretched from Thrace to the borders of India, spreading Greek culture (Hellenism) across the Near East, Persia, and Central Asia.

Seleucus I received Babylon after the 311 BCE Settlement of Triparadisus and built his capital at Antioch-on-the-Orontes (modern Antakya, Turkey) in 300 BCE, founding dozens of new Greek cities including Seleucia, Apamea, and Laodicea. The empire's multicultural Hellenistic character — Greek ruling class over Persian, Babylonian, Syrian, and Jewish subjects — created the cultural synthesis that later Roman Syria and Byzantium inherited. The Seleucid calendar, beginning in 312 BCE, was used by Jewish and Arabic communities for centuries.

Seleucid conflict with the Maccabees in Judea (producing Hanukkah) and the gradual independence of Bactria, Parthia, and Judea under regional rulers eroded the empire. Rome's defeat of Antiochus III at Magnesia in 190 BCE broke Seleucid power in Asia Minor. The empire shrank to Syria, Phoenicia, and Mesopotamia before Tigranes of Armenia and Pompey of Rome completed its dissolution by 63 BCE.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Seleucid Empire spread Hellenism from Syria to Bactria, creating the cultural synthesis that bridged Greek and Persian civilizations and shaped Judaism, Christianity, and Islam through its Hellenistic legacy.
